terms.grammar: adverb; mostly with the verb of the question repeated
evidence: Ter. Eun. 850–853: Satin' id tibi placet? — Nōn.
Cic. Ac. 2.104: aut etiam aut nōn respondēre (Lewis & Short s.v. nōn)
terms.comment: Latin has no single word for “no”. The plainest answer repeats the verb with nōn (“Are you staying? — I’m not staying”), or is nōn alone, Cicero’s pair to etiam (see yes).

evidence: Ter. Hec. 5.3.16: Sed cessās? — Minimē equidem (Lewis & Short s.v. parvus)
terms.comment: The emphatic negative answer, “by no means”; stronger still minimē gentium (see no way!).

evidence: Cic. Tusc. 1.10: An tū haec nōn crēdis? — Minimē vērō. (Lewis & Short s.v. parvus)
Traupman 22: minimē vērō hercle!, heck no!
Plaut. Most. 3.1.19: Etiam fatētur dē hospite? — Immō pernegat. (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: never, like minimē, an answer on its own; it brings the clause that corrects the question (see actually).

phrases.english: Tell me, did you run away? — Yes, ma’am. — Are you pleased with that? — No.

phrases.latin: Satin' sīc est? — Nōn. — Quid sī sīc? — Propemodum. — Quid sī sīc? — Sat est.
phrases.english: Is this all right? — No. — How about this? — Nearly. — And this? — That’ll do.
